newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan president sacks former ally Bhutto.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan president sacks former ally Bhutto.

text.p: Pakistani President Farooq Leghari dismissed Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto on Tuesday, wielding constitutional powers he once said should be clipped.

"I am satisfied that a situation has arisen in which the Government of the Federation cannot be carried on in accordance with the provisions of the Constitution, and an appeal to the electorate is necessary," Leghari said in a proclamation ousting Bhutto and dissolving the National Assembly (lower house).
He named former parliament speaker Meraj Khalid, 80, as caretaker prime minister to supervise general elections he said would be held on February 3.
Leghari, an Oxford-educated tribal chief from Punjab province, began his five-year term in November 1993, a month after Bhutto's Pakistan People's Party (PPP) won general elections.
A former PPP secretary-general and Bhutto ally, Leghari said the day before being sworn in that presidential powers to dissolve the National Assembly should be curbed.
"The Sword of Damocles hanging over the parliament of presidential dissolution must be removed," he said. "I feel I can play a crucial role in stabilising democracy."

The power to dissolve the assembly was given to the president under the controversial Eighth Amendment to the constitution, introduced by former military ruler President Mohammad Zia-ul-Haq in 1985 and later approved by the assembly.

The PPP and the main opposition Pakistan Muslim League (PML) both oppose the amendment, which has been used three times to oust elected governments, but have failed to come together to provide the two-thirds majority in the house needed to undo it.
The PPP-nominated Leghari, a bureaucrat-turned-politician, as its presidential candidate only after the PML turned down Bhutto's offer to put forward a consensus nominee.
Leghari, then still a Bhutto loyalist, weathered early opposition attacks on his integrity and impartiality.
The PML had accused the president, previously one of the few Pakistani politicians with a reputation for honesty, of selling land to the collapsed Mehran Bank at inflated prices.
Leghari denied the charge and sued his detractors, waiving presidential prerogatives to appear personally in court.
The opposition campaign climaxed in October 1994 when PML deputies shouted him down at the formal opening of parliament, which dissolved into chaos as rival members scuffled.
Leghari, a tall, upright figure, kept his dignity, and his even-handed policy towards government and opposition eventually convinced the PML to tone down its attempts to denigrate him.
An ethnic Baloch from Dera Ghazi Khan, in rural Punjab province bordering Balochistan, Leghari is a feudal landowner with a strong Moslem faith. He speaks Balochi, Pashtu, Punjabi, Urdu and English.

Unlike many of his fellow landowners, Leghari is a firm advocate of taxing agricultural income. Though an avowed supporter of privatisation, he opposed the sale of state-run Oil and Gas Development Corporation on national security grounds.
He backed Bhutto's drive to attract foreign investment and was instrumental in persuading Hong Kong-based tycoon Gordon Wu to invest in Pakistan's energy sector.
Leghari was water and power minister in Bhutto's first government from 1988 to 1990 before she was sacked by former president Ghulam Ishaq Khan.
He was one of Bhutto's key lieutenants during her 1992 "Long March" to topple the PML government led by Nawaz Sharif.
Leghari orchestrated PPP backing for then president Ghulam Ishaq Khan when he mustered support in April 1992 to sack Sharif on charges similar to those he had used to dismiss Bhutto.
Educated at the renowned Aitchison College in Lahore and at Oxford, Leghari entered the civil service in 1963, serving in the former East Pakistan, now Bangladesh.
He quit 10 years later to join the PPP at the invitation of Bhutto's father -- Pakistan's first popularly elected prime minister, Zulfikar Ali Bhutto -- and entered the Senate in 1975.
Two years later he won a National Assembly seat and was briefly minister of production before Zia ousted Bhutto.

Leghari spent four years in jail under Zia's martial law government before re-entering the National Assembly in the 1988 elections that followed Zia's death in a mysterious plane crash that year and brought Benazir Bhutto to office.
Leghari, a keen hunter and hiker, is married with two sons and two daughters.
